title: How do you stop the load balancer itself from being a single point of failure (redundant pairs/failover, health checks, DNS failover)?
shortTitle: How do you stop the load balancer itself from being a single point of failure?
keyPoints: A single load balancer is a SPOF: if it dies, backends are unreachable even though they are healthy.
Active-passive pair: two nodes share a floating virtual IP (VIP); VRRP/keepalived manages heartbeat failover.
Active-active: both nodes serve traffic; DNS or upstream distributes across both VIPs.
DNS failover: Route 53 health checks stop returning an unreachable zone's address; bounded by TTL caching.
Managed cloud load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP, Azure) are internally redundant and span multiple AZs.
Stateless load balancing simplifies failover; sticky-session tables complicate it.
Always test the failover; an untested standby often fails when needed.

s1_definition.oneliner: Never run one load balancer; run a redundant pair sharing a floating virtual IP with heartbeat failover, add health checks, and use DNS or multi-zone failover so the loss of any single balancer never takes the system down.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Redundant pair** -- two load balancer nodes share a floating virtual IP (VIP); the active node serves and the passive takes over on failure.
- **VRRP/keepalived** -- a protocol that manages the VIP: nodes exchange heartbeats and the passive takes the VIP if the active stops.
- **Active-active** -- both nodes serve traffic simultaneously; uses DNS or upstream distribution.
- **DNS failover** -- health checks stop returning an unreachable zone's address; bounded by TTL caching.
- **Managed cloud LBs** -- internally redundant, multi-AZ services; not a single box.
- **Test failover** -- an untested standby often fails when needed.
s1_definition.analogy: The floor manager at National Bank of India directs every customer, but if there is only one manager and they faint, the branch jams. The fix: two managers sharing the same badge (VIP). They check on each other constantly, and the instant the active one faints, the standby grabs the badge. At the city level, if one whole branch is unreachable, customers are sent to another (DNS failover).

sections.s6_takeaway:
The irony of load balancing is that if you are not careful you simply move the single point of failure from the backends to the load balancer. All traffic flows through it, so if it dies the whole system is unreachable even though every backend is healthy.

The primary fix is a redundant pair sharing a floating VIP with heartbeat failover. VRRP via keepalived has the nodes exchange heartbeats, and when the active stops the passive takes the VIP within seconds. DNS failover covers zone and region outages: health checks stop returning a dead zone's address. Managed cloud LBs are internally redundant and span multiple AZs, handling most of this automatically.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj ran an active-passive pair with a VIP for sub-second in-zone failover, and Route 53 health-checked DNS for multi-zone coverage. The most important lesson was to always test the failover, because an untested standby often fails when needed.

Remember one sentence: never run a single load balancer; run a redundant pair with a floating VIP for fast in-zone failover, add DNS failover for zone outages, lean on managed multi-AZ load balancers in the cloud, and always test the failover.
